source.title: Genome-Wide Prediction of Complex Traits in Two Outcrossing Plant Species Through Deep Learning and Bayesian Regularized Neural Network
source.authors: Carlos Maldonado; Freddy Mora-Poblete; R. Contreras-Soto; Sunny Ahmar; Jen-Tsung Chen; A. T. Do Amaral; C. Scapim

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears to contain the full paper.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates mini-batch size using held-out predictive ability in maize and eucalypt breeding populations, extending batch-size findings to genomic prediction of plant traits. It does not measure the training–test error gap directly.
record.gate_note: The paper tests batch size and activation-function combinations in LSTM models and reports validation predictive ability. It does not test arbitrary-label memorization, model width, convolutional versus fully connected architectures, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removing memorized examples.
record.test_reason: The study compares batch sizes for genomic phenotype prediction, but the supplied text does not establish a fixed epoch budget or a controlled comparison of training budgets. Its results therefore cannot establish V5's conditional batch-size effect. It discusses prior large-batch generalization findings. Held-out predictive ability is a relevant performance measure; the absence of a training–test gap measure is not itself grounds for exclusion.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately captures the authors' main conclusion: ReLU with a large batch was the preferred tested LSTM configuration, and the selected DL model achieved the highest reported predictive ability across the study traits. Superiority was not statistically significant in every comparison. The authors also propose estimating DL marker effects through an iterative algorithm for identifying genomic regions.
record.recipe_differences: The study predicts natural plant phenotypes with LSTM and Bayesian regularized neural networks and compares validation predictive ability; it does not use random-label memorization experiments or measure training–test error gaps.
record.method_sensitivity: Predictive ability varied with activation function and mini-batch size; the authors report that ReLU performed better as mini-batch size increased, with trait- and population-specific patterns.

fits_no_version.finding: With ReLU, increasing the batch from 10% to 100% of the training set significantly improves validation Pearson correlation for all five eucalypt traits. Epoch budgets are unspecified.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger batches can improve held-out genomic phenotype prediction in the tested LSTM configurations.

record.problems: Validation predictive ability is not a direct measure of the training–test error gap. The supplied results do not report training error or a fixed epoch budget, and no arbitrary-label condition is tested.
record.rows_left_out: Rows for the other LSTM configurations (lstm2, lstm3, lstm4, lstm6), maize traits, and BRNN architectures are omitted because the extraction is limited to the 10 ReLU 10%-versus-100% mini-batch eucalypt comparisons. Table 1 contains additional LSTM results; Table 2 contains BRNN results.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and dependence on tuning.
Large-batch performance under an established fixed epoch budget; image and language workloads; recovery through longer training or recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and interactions with data size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Other batch configurations and maize results are explicitly declared in rows_left_out, so they are not missing extractions. The study is not an original source for any listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image models and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning and regularization recipes.
Fixed epoch budgets, image-classification and language benchmarks, and whether training for longer or adapting the recipe removes a generalization-gap penalty.
Dropout and its interaction with training-set size and data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with the training–test error gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
